- When sentiment shows strong positive momentum (e.g., >0.67) followed by a sharp decline, model tends to over-forecast and overshoots; reduce forecast by 1–2% in such cases.
- If sentiment turns negative (e.g., <0.33) or shows strong downward change, model often under-responds; increase forecast slightly to counteract mean reversion bias.
- After a recent spike in sentiment or price, model frequently overreacts in the next 3–5 days; apply a 1–3% downward correction to prevent overshoot.
- When sentiment is flat or neutral (e.g., 0.33–0.67) and news volume is steady, model tends to drift toward historical mean; adjust forecast to align with recent 7–14 day average.
- If sentiment change is negative and news volume is high, model often fails to adjust quickly; apply a 1–2% upward correction to avoid underestimating volatility.
- For 30-day horizon, model consistently overestimates early in the cycle (first 5–7 days) when sentiment is rising; reduce forecast by 1–3% for first 5 days if sentiment is trending up.
- If sentiment is consistently low (e.g., <0.33) and price is trending down, model often underestimates the drop; increase forecast by 1–2% to account for mean reversion or policy-driven corrections.
